extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers learning how to form and evaluate scientific hypotheses
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for creating, testing, and accepting scientific hypotheses, including the logical role of hypotheses in induction and deduction, what makes a hypothesis legitimate or vicious, and how hypotheses should lead to verifiable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: An hypothesis is any supposition which we make (either without actual evidence, or on evidence avowedly insufficient) in order to endeavour to deduce from it conclusions in accordance with facts which are known to be real; under the idea that if the conclusions to which the hypothesis leads are known truths, the hypothesis itself either must be, or at least is likely to be, true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses are invented to enable the Deductive Method to be earlier applied to phenomena; their principal purpose is to supply a provisional premise from which deductive consequences can be worked out and compared with observed facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tri-partite requirement for deductive identification of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: To discover the cause of any phenomenon by the Deductive Method, the process must consist of three parts; induction, ratiocination, and verification. No one of these three parts of the process can be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction: ascertain laws of causes. Ratiocination: compute from those laws how causes operate in the particular case. Verification: compare calculated effect with actual phenomenon. All three must be present for a complete deductive proof (example: Newton's identification of lunar/terrestrial gravity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy condition for the Hypothetical Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hypothetical Method (which assumes a law instead of proving it by induction) is legitimate only if the final step, the verification, shall amount to, and fulfil the conditions of, a complete induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires assurance that no other law except the assumed one could deductively lead to the same true results — i.e., a false law cannot lead to the same true conclusions. When that uniqueness holds, a hypothesis can become a proved law by verification (example: Newton's derivation of Kepler's laws from inverse-square assumption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of both positive and negative instances (Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification must supply both the affirmative instance (that from the hypothesis we can deduce the known facts) and the negative instance (that no other antecedent, except the one assumed in the hypothesis, would in conjunction with the background produce the same effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without both instances one cannot claim the hypothesis is established; Newton's argument illustrated obtaining the negative instance by showing alternative hypotheses would give different results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa / independent evidential demonstrability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a condition of a genuinely scientific hypothesis that the supposed cause should be something actually existing in nature whose existence should be capable of being detected, and its connexion with the effect ascribed to it should be susceptible of being proved by independent evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's maxim that the cause assigned must be a 'vera causa' is interpreted to mean the cause need not be previously known, but must be capable of later independent proof (example: the luminiferous ether would gain standing if independently evidenced by e.g. accumulated resistive effects on planetary motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testability / potential to be proved or disproved
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis should not be destined always to remain an hypothesis, but be of such a nature as to be either proved or disproved by comparison with observed facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses that cannot in principle be tested or converted into proved facts (because no observations/experiments could ever detect their truth or falsity) are epistemically weak or 'vicious' (example: Cartesian vortices were vicious because their reality could not be conclusively tested).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis must suggest feasible lines of investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The hypothesis, by suggesting observations and experiments, puts us on the road to independent evidence if it be really attainable; and till it be attained, the hypothesis ought not to count for more than a conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A useful hypothesis directs empirical work — even if initially conjectural, it should generate testable predictions or experiments that could provide independent evidence (illustrated by how speculative hypotheses led to experiments in optics and planetary motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hypotheses about laws of known causes vs hypotheses introducing unknown causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the hypothesis relates to the cause or mode of production of a phenomenon, it is different whether the cause is already ascertained or is wholly imaginary; the former can often be verified by showing alternative laws would produce different results, whereas the latter requires that the suggested new cause be capable of independent proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses about the precise law governing a known cause are stronger candidates for acceptance via the Hypothetical Method than hypotheses that posit an entirely new, previously unknown agent (Newton's work vs. speculative unknown causes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive success is supportive but not conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: That a hypothesis has led to the anticipation and prediction of others which experience afterwards verified is evidence in its favour, but not conclusive proof of its truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple successful predictions increase plausibility, but identical or similar laws can arise from distinct mechanisms; therefore prediction alone doesn't establish the real underlying mechanism (discussion of undulatory theory of light vs emission theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid acceptance merely because no alternative is imagined
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a valid reason for accepting any hypothesis that we are unable to imagine any other which will account for the facts; the true explanation may be one we cannot currently conceive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inability to conceive alternatives (due to limited experience) does not amount to evidence that the conceived hypothesis is true; historical counterexamples exist where different mechanistic accounts later appeared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and iterative correction (practical heuristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest supposition which accords with the more obvious facts is the best to begin with; this rude hypothesis is then corrected and the operation repeated until deductive results tally with phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple provisional hypotheses as starting points because their consequences are easiest to trace; refine them iteratively in light of discrepancies (compared to Methods of Approximation in mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical plausibility but not decisive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses which ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature have plausibility, but analogy alone does not prove identity of mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis that mirrors the laws of some known class of phenomena (e.g., undulatory motions like vibrations of elastic fluids) can suggest experiments, yet analogous laws can arise from distinct causes (examples: inverse-square laws occur in gravitation, illumination, and heat diffusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses that only represent or describe phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical modes of merely representing or describing phenomena (e.g., epicycles, circles, excentrics) are forms of hypothesis that may be retained until verified; they are hypotheses until they are confirmed by facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive hypotheses can be useful as interim models, but remain provisional until verification provides independent evidence (Kepler's successive guesses about orbits are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/forensic/geological inference without new-agent hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: When inferring past causes from present effects (geology, forensic inquiries), if the effect corresponds exactly to what known causes produce and no other known cause could have generated the effect, one may conclude the known cause acted in the past without speculative hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is legitimate induction based on uniformities (e.g., identifying deposits as aqueous or igneous origins) and differs from inventing new agents; such inferences need not rely on speculative hypotheses when existing agents suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses that are unverifiable remain conjectural and should be treated accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: If a hypothesis suggests an unknown agent but cannot lead to any course of investigation capable of converting it from hypothesis into a proved fact, it remains a mere conjecture and should not be treated as established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cartesian vortices (disproved by cometary motion evidence) and speculative ether hypotheses prior to independent evidence; useful for generating thought but not for claiming truth.
